review_text_raw:
Hack the Planet!!

I was a fan of Uplink back in the day, but it is certainly time for a modern quality release! I streamed Hacknet for 5 hours the other night and we had a great time experiencing what the world had to offer. You would think I rocketed through the game faster, but honestly much of the time was spent messing around in servers and poking around. The intuitive gameplay, explorable content, and the way the game handles failure made for a really enjoyable experience. 

One thing I enjoyed was how intiutive everything was. This isn't linux, this isn't MS-DOS, this isn't even hacking per se. It's an adventure game with a command line interface. Hacking concepts and tools are abstracted for playablilty though it should be noted that there are some real hacking suites out there that are scarily easier to use then what you find in the game.

I'd love to go into details about the exciting things I found, but half of the fun is exploring. One big suggestion I have is to read through the help command in your OS - all 3 pages. Your HacknetOS has a lot of functionality that you wouldn't normally expect. The commands can also let you have a lot of fun! I had a ball changing some IRC logs and websites to include my viewers names to much embarassment and laughs. 

An aspect I appreciated is that the punishment for making mistakes is firm but fair. Going into too much detail would be spoiling, but suffice it to say don't just get cozy clicking on the GUI for everything you do. Know your commands and they will treat you well in return.

I did encounter a few minor bugs, some graphic glitches dealing with text, however none were game breaking and I documented this information back to the company. At the stage I'm at in the game there were no hardware upgrades, but I have uncovered a number of hacking tools to provide alternate forms of entry into more difficult servers.

I'm happy to share more of my experience with you, or if you'd like just stop by the channel to see it in action.

DISCLAIMER: I was provided a pre-relase copy of the game by Surprise Attack Games with no additional compensation or influence. Heck I like the game so much I'm picking up a copy to give away to my viewers. :)


EDIT:  After a few more streams of the game, and now about 15 more hours spent with Hacknet I'm still loving the experience  The universe is solid, with some very interesting servers you encounter that make homages to pop culture and game references in some instances.  The banter logs are proabably my favorite things to hunt down as it makes it feel a little more real that people are using these boxes.

As for those miffed about me talking about my stream?  I respect your thumbs down, but potential buyers got to see Hacknet in action and it helped them make a purchasing decision (lots of YES!).  Totally worth it.

review_text_raw:
This is gonna be a lengthy review. I'll add a TL;DR at the bottom.

When I first went to view the page for this game, there were many questions that began flooding my mind. And now that I've played the game almost to its entirety, I think that I can answer most of these questions that interested consumers passing by may have. This game was a real treat, and I think that it deserves more attention than it's received.


[h1] Is Hacknet realistic? [/h1]

If you mean "realistic" as in "Is this game close to hacking in real life?" then the answer is no. This game is not realistic because it is fun and doesn't make you paranoid. You are in possession of a bunch of hacking tools that put up the kinds of graphics you'd expect to be running on computers in a 90's hacker film, and the way these tools work is by executing them and waiting for the flashy hacking graphics to stop flashing so that you can run another flashy hacker tool until you gain administrative system access. Granted, it's more complex than that, which is why this game is really enjoyable, but you're not going to be writing complex algorithms to overload proxy servers and bypass tracing measures. That's what the 90's tools are for.

That being said, this may be as close as gaming will ever come to realistic hacking. Because anything that tries to be precicely like real hacking that doesn't give you fancy hacker programs probably isn't going to be a very fun game. And this, again, is a fun game. The entire game takes place on a computer's operating system, and every hack you perform is done through this system. In addition, the commands you use are based on real UNIX commands, even if the commands are typically used to activate the previously-mentioned hacking programs. It's certainly more realistic than games where you push a button and your character goes [i]"I'm in" [/i] like Watch_Dogs and Quadrilateral Cowboy (That isn't to say that they're bad games, just that they're not trying to be realistic hacking simulations which, again, isn't necessarily a bad thing).


[h1] Is this game immersive? Will I feel like a hacker even if I'm not performing real hacks? [/h1]

Oh, yes. If you want to feel like the genius hacker that always appears in Hollywood films but rarely gets any time for actual character development, then this game is for you. The presentation of this game is great, and it really helps to sell that feeling of accomplishment that you get when you pull off a successful job. After about 30 minutes in, I had to re-check the steam store to make sure that I wasn't accessing a multiplayer hacking simulator. But nope, I was even able to play this game in airplane mode. As the store page mentions, there are very few things that break the immersion by being obvious parts of a video game. To complete a job, you email the client explaining that you've finished. To acquire a new tool, you have to copy said tool to your home computer from its rightful owner. 

And this immersive presentation goes a long way in the overall experience. I know that not everybody responds the same way, but I found certain parts to incite genuine emotion in a way that few other games have managed to pull off. Like when you're given the option to accept a job in which [spoiler]you have to euthanize a dying man by hacking his pacemaker [/spoiler], or when [spoiler]you run "OpenCDtray" on your own system and your real computer's disc tray opens and may potentially scare the hell out of you[/spoiler]. So even if you're using overpowered tools to open systems that nobody bothers to check, you'll probably still feel really good doing so.


[h1] Do I need to know coding or hacking in order to understand this game? [/h1]

No, you don't. The tutorial explains everything pretty well, and it makes sure that you understand how the systems work before even thinking about letting you out into the hacking world. No coding is required (I'm not even sure if coding algorithms is possible with the interface), and most of the game's difficulty comes with memorizing the commands and executing them at the appropriate times. That being said, if you don't know a whole lot about computers, the most difficult task will probably be [spoiler] getting your interface back after being locked to terminal mode by another hacker [/spoiler]. But if you experiment enough, then you'll ususally find the solutions to most of the challenges, and there are plenty of walkthroughs and tips out there if you end up getting desperate. But I was able to finish the game with little prior programming experience. If you know how to navigate a computer's interface or have downloaded and fixed mods on to other games, then you'll probably be fine with this game. Just, you know, don't delete important files or screw up on a trace aversion. I don't know if this game prevents you from screwing yourself over, and everybody's too scared to find out.


[h1] Is the game worth ten bucks? [/h1]

Yeah, I'd say so. You'll probably get around 10 hours out of it if you're doing the main story without any outside assitance, 14-15 hours if you're also doing the labrynths DLC. I'd say that it's not everybody's cup of tea; surely, your relative who spends all day exclusively playing [i] Fortnite [/i] would probably get turned off by this, but odds are you're at least mildly interested in this game if you're reading this review right now, considering that this game gets talked about as much as what brand of toilet paper you prefer when you're finished up on the toilet. So yeah, I'd recommend this game to anybody reading this review.


[h1] Oh, boy. It's one of those games that tries to sell its soundtrack as DLC. Is it good enough to warrant a purchase? [/h1]

I was honestly surprised by this game's soundtrack. Again, I understand that everybody has different tastes in music, but I found this particular OST track good to write and do homework to. It felt really good to listen to in-game while hacking servers and computers. The music is used as sort of an indicator on what part of the game you're currently at, and when the song changes, you know you're probably making progress. I found that [spoiler] Roller Mobster by Carpenter Brut [/spoiler] fit this game better than it did for HM2. That being said, I haven't purchased the soundtrack since most of it is available on YouTube anyways. And yes, it's ten dollars. Fifteen dollars for the main game and DLC soundtrack. So while I'll admit that the soundtrack is pretty good, I'd only spend the extra fifteen bucks if you like having the songs directly at your fingertips at all times.


[h1] TL;DR [/h1]

This is a great game that may be as close to realistic hacking as gaming will come while still remaining enjoyable. The presentation and aeshetic really add a lot to it, and you don't need to be experienced with programming or hacking in order to complete it. It's worth the money and gives around 10 hours of playtime assuming you don't mess up massively and have to start a new game. I'm gonna give this a thumbs up, and I wish it came out later so that I could put it in my favorite 2018 games list.

review_text_raw:
[b]DISCLAIMER: I was provided a press review copy for the purposes of documenting the game for PCGamingWiki, a publicly-editable technical wiki for games.[/b]

What would happen if you gamified the idea that you found a copy of an OS which was so dead-simple to use, anyone with basic computer and investigative skills could hack into [i]anything[/i]? You'd get Hacknet, an excellent hacking game designed to be the spiritual successor to Uplink. Slick graphics, a sliding difficulty designed to get you introduced to the game's mechancis one-by-one, and an in-the-background story which is surprisingly pointient and explores not only how insecure computers really are to a dedicated hacker, but the ramifications, both practical and mornal, of an OS designed to hack anything.

[b]TL;DR:[/b] It's a short, satisfying hacking game which, despite how complicated it seems at the outset, eases you into its mechanics, world, and story, and gives you the surprising, satisfying feeling of being both a master hacker and Sherlock Holmes at the same time.

[h1]Is this Uplink 2.0?[/h1]
For the mandatory "Is this Uplink 2.0" part of the review: no. This is [i]not[/i] the spiritual successor hardcore fans of Uplink have been looking for because:
[list]
[*] You use a 'real' computer with fixed specs, with HacknetOS running on top of it as a VM (Virtual Machine).
[*] The game is command-line based with some GUI helpers, such as an IP map, optional GUI-based system navigation, and a note app.
[*] You can only run computer-compromising apps via command-line.
[*] The game's story, despite being subtle, in the background, and without limitations (i.e. x number of connections before game over), drives the game, and your actions are ultimately in service of the story.
[/list]

If none of the above scared you off, then read on because this spiritual sequel is, in spite of the above, a worthy one IMO...
[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
As mentioned above, Hacknet uses its command-line for much of the hacking, with a few GUI helpers for those tasks too cumbersome to exclusively do in the GUI, like keeping track of all the known IPs and keeping notes. Despite this, there are only a few core commands, and are remarkably easy-to-remember with repeated use - and the game is [i]very[/i] careful to ensure you do - and often relate to what they do. For example, to crack an in-game computer's SSH port, run SSHcrack [insert port number here]. This is further helped by the addition of command auto-completion - something the game teaches you how to use very quickly. So, that SSHcrack command I just mentioned? All you really need to type in is SSH, press the TAB key, add the port number, and press the Enter key. Believe me - it makes your life a [i]lot[/i] easier.

The hacking itself is simple: connect to the target, probe the computer for weaknesses, then execute programs to exploit their weaknesses. Some computers require some preperatory work, such as computers with proxies effectively require you to use other computers you've compromised to attack them, while others might require you to find a piece of cracking software to open them up, bypass a firewall by running special software to solve its encryption, and so on. At first, it isn't so difficult - just run the apps, and watch the magic happen. Later on, you'll begin to regularly encounter computers which will attempt to passively hunt your computer down and force it to reboot - complete with a giant timer showing you the exact time to failure - requiring you to run multiple apps at once. Since your computer only has so much memory, you'll need to play Tetris with the apps, shutting down those you don't need and running the ones which bypass the easiest weaknessess. Beating the clock and compromising a computer with a second to spare is an accomplishment in an of itself which never gets old.

Another good thing is the game understands how counter-intuitive command-line use is for the average user, so through the use of an initial tutorial (which can be skipped once you know how to terminate it) and missions which slowly slide up in difficulty as they teach the basic mechanics, you'll eventually come to grips with the commands you need to hack. And once you do, it starts giving you missions which, combined with the clear, clever visuals (more on those later), allow you to feel like a master hacker in a way different from other hacking games because you'll often need to do something which most hacking games leave out entirely or towards the very end.

[b]You get to be Sherlock Holmes.[/b]

You see, because people, even those with good security sense, tend to forget or excuse security issues, they also tend to leave stuff on their computers, mobile devices, and e-mail accounts. IP addresses to secret files, administrator (admin) passwords for top-secret servers and their most private e-mails - you name it, they'll leave it. As such, any good hacker needs to dig through files to find all those details so they can find what they need with the least amount of effort - allowing you to find hidden servers, open files which would otherwise be closed to you, and skip dangerous, time-consuming, and sometimes impossible system hacks by simply logging in as the administrator. You'll be surprised how satisfied you'll feel following a trail of clues to your ultimate objective, making an impossible task suddenly seem trivial - and end up finding some hilarious stuff in the process as you dig through all the files which don't matter.

All that said, there are some things which make the game easier than it should be. A key part of the gameplay is erasing anything in the system's logs indicating you were there so the authorities can't track your hacks back to you. In theory, this means deleting every log file before leaving the server; in practice, all you have to do in most cases is start deleting all the log files, disconnect from the server, wait for all the files to be deleted, then come back. "How can I delete files from a computer I just disconnected from?" you ask. You shouldn't, but the game lets you. This means that as long as the computer doesn't have a rotating admin password - and most don't - what should be down-to-the-wire hacks end up being trivial. Furthermore, any future accessing of the computer will be ignored - even if you never delete the logs after the first time.

Oddly enough, that one problem with the gameplay is...actually a bonus in my eyes, since it enables you to focus more on solving the challenging Sherlock Holmes-esque puzzles.
[h1]Story[/h1]
I can't really touch on the story much as to do so would ruin the surprise and horror it provides late in the game. I can say, though, that the story, while simple, is quite sophisticated, as it explores through your actions just what kind of power HacknetOS gives those who own it in today's digital age, where everything - and I do mean [i]everything[/i] - is connected to the Internet and, thus, can be compromised, pried open, and tampered with.
[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The graphics in Hacknet are very minimalistic and clean, meaning you can see exactly what's what with minimal effort. There are also some optional, subtle effects which emulate a CRT computer monitor, adding to the realism. The standout graphics come from the apps, as they show you in fun and clever ways how they're progressing, whether it shows you punching through an SSH table with every section hacked turned green or beat out an SMTP mail server's sorting algorithm to force it to shut down and open up to you.
[h1]Additional Thoughts[/h1]
I really wish the game opened up towards the middle - it would've been fun exploring the world wide web, finding hidden sub-plots as you tear through the world's computers like tissue paper, as a reprieve from the short story. Speaking of the story, I also wish it were longer - the game's puzzles were clever and unique, and I so desperately wanted more content.

I can say, though, that the story, while simple, is quite sophisticated, as it explores through your actions just what kind of power HacknetOS gives those who own it in today's digital age, where everything - and I do mean [i]everything[/i] - is connected to the Internet and, thus, can be compromised, pried open, and tampered with. [h1]Graphics[/h1] The graphics in Hacknet are very minimalistic and clean, meaning you can see exactly what's what with minimal effort. review_text_raw:
Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

review_text_raw:
I don’t know why it’s taken me so long to get around to playing Hacknet, but now I’m kicking myself for not playing it sooner. I have not felt this engaged in an investigative simulation since I played The Black Watchmen and I really hope to find more games like this.

Hacknet is definitely a game for certain types of people, but you don’t need to have extensive IT experience to play. I think gamers who are already comfortable using command prompt will feel at home with this sim, but the game’s tutorial does a good job of walking you through the concepts and gameplay basics while still leaving you free to get creative with how to implement the tools at your disposal. Nobody is going to learn to be a [i]real[/i] hacker by playing this game, but it’s a fun introduction to the ideas behind the process and it’s immersive enough that you feel like you’re really involved with the story.

Hacknet is at its core a mystery game and your task is to track down what happened to a mysterious person who contacts you. As you work your way across the shadowy world of IP addresses, you are given more abilities and greater challenges to tinker with. I never felt that any of the tasks were impossible -- it was always that I just missed something or overlooked a scan or available command. Fast typists will have a much easier time of playing as there are frequent timers counting down in the guise of tracers.

I absolutely 100% recommend that you pick up the DLC Labyrinths. It pretty much adds an entire game campaign where you get to expand on your skills using new situations. You can play the DLC any time while still keeping your progress with the main game. Seriously, worth the extra few bucks if you can swing it.

I'd recommend this game - but you should ready below!

I'd like to address the most common question I see floating around first. YES, you absolutely can play this game without any knowledge of cybersecurity, programming, coding languages, etc. The tutorial is short but good IMO - watching a few videos online can be helpful but it's optional. 
You basically run the same loop of commands the entire game, it just get more complicated as you go - but the foundation is the same. 

With that out of the way, let's address the elephant in the room.
IF YOU HAVE A MAC RUNNING ON M CHIPS - DO NOT BUY!

Unfortunately, this game does not perform will on MacOS with M chips. I have a M3 Pro and the game crashes randomly every 2 - 10 minutes. And this is a real shame.
I have tried joining the official discord to speak to the developer, but it's pretty clear that the game has been abandoned. 

If you are running on Windows, then this is a gem of a game and you should definitely buy it. I never knew these kind of games could be so much fun. 
If you are a Mac user, don't waste your money :(

review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] I played this offline, but i think it took somewhere around 12-24h to finish the game.
[b]Grindy Achievement:[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement:[/b] Yes (8 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement:[/b] No.
[b]Developer Response:[/b] No (last response is in 26 Feb, 2019).

[h1]Intro[/h1]
Hacknet is a hacking simulator game where you have to hack some ip address with the tools you had. Most of the hacking will be done through terminal although the game has some GUI that you can interact with.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Even though i said that you'll type your commands through terminal, it doesn't mean that you'll only have to look at it. There are some UI in the game that you can see, such as when you launch your tools or check the compromised system. I even think that the UI helped very well because i'm sure i don't want to browse all of the system directory from the command line; it took too much effort to type and check them all. You can also see the server location and connect to them without typing at all in case you forgot the ip or just too lazy to type the whole thing.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The game's story is mostly told through an exchange of emails and reading files in a server. You'll investigate someone who has been lost for a long time, Bit, while uncovering a hidden secret that causes his disappearance. The story might look decent, but i'm quite impressed with the visuals at the end of the story.

The game also has additional files in the servers that you hacked in. I like to read some of them (especially the short ones) since they are pretty funny.

[h1]The game[/h1]
As a hacking simulator game, the game simulates the terminal very well. The basic is pretty much the same (ls, cd, cat, etc) while there are some custom commands mixed in. The game also has an auto complete feature although it's quite limited; you can't do auto complete for stuffs in other directory. Well, sometimes it works, but sometimes it don't. The game also doesn't support complicated command with arguments like rm -rf (remove everything in a directory) even though the game has missions like this. The limitations are pretty acceptable to me though.

Anyway, if you have no idea with anything that i said above, the game will help you to learn some terminal commands. If you're in windows, it's the thing that popped up when you press windows+r and then type cmd, except that the commands are for Linux OS and the like. Like how most terminals are, there is a help command that you can use to recognize all of the available commands and if you didn't notice it like i did, the help command actually has paging in it; you can type help 1, help 2, and help 3 to check most of the commands in the game. Most, because the help command won't tell you anything about what does your .exe file do.

Beside the basic commands, you'll also have .exe files. These files are usually what is installed in your computer and can be basically anything, from a browser to your game. However, most .exe files in this game is actually a tool that is used for hacking. You'll know how the things work if you read the instructions, which is obviously stored somewhere else. You'll usually get these .exe files by going through some servers and copying the files to your machine.

In this game, you'll need to read a lot. By a lot, i mean a lot. Really. You might need to understand some complicated stuffs or just know the general knowledge and the game will punish you severely if you don't know what are you doing. I mistook proxy servers and port for a while and i thought that i need 4 proxy servers to hack in a server although it actually asked me to open 4 ports. I got confused for a while before i noticed my mistake.

Sometimes, the game won't tell you what to do and you had to understand everything by yourself. One example is when a hacker suddenly attacked me. I didn't know what to do at that point because the tutorial (yes, there is a tutorial) only tells me how to hack.

As i said before, you'll usually hack a server. You'll have a lead in a form of ip address that you need to hack in and you'll check what you need to do to hack it. The game will usually tell you whether you have to connect to a proxy, guess a firewall, run one of your hacking tools to open a number of port required to get in, or all of them. Sometimes, the server owner will notice your break in and a timer will show up. You must finish your hacking, remove your traces, and logout before it reaches zero or you'll get a blue screen. The strange thing is, the game is a bit "buggy" on this. If you leave the server while running your hacking tools, the hacking will still be ongoing and you can do your second attempt with a head start. The stranger thing is, if the timer reach zero by the time you finish the hacking (and you haven't logged out yet), the hacking will also be finished after you deal with the blue screen and return to the server. Well, there are actually some more, but these two are the only thing that i had in my mind for now.

Since you'll use a lot of hacking tools, you might run out of memories. Some hacking tools take more memories than the others so you can't use them all at the same time. This helps to make the game more difficult although there is one place where you have to "cheat" your way through because you will never have the time to get in in the first place [spoiler](the CCC Hacksquad Filedump)[/spoiler].

The game's story has a two branching paths that will converge in the end. The other path requires you to really know what you're doing though; i won't be able to make it in if i didn't read a guide beforehand. The game also has some commands that are not available in help commands that might be useful in these cases. These additional commands are told after you beat the game and is supposed to be an additional command in case there is a new update in.

You'll mostly play the game by accepting quests and finishing them. There is also a few points in the game where you can choose the missions that you want to do. Sadly, there is a place where you can't choose them all and it kinda saddens me since it left the place with unfinished tasks.

Since you'll be hacking a lot of servers, there are some optional places that you can go to and some places might have some secrets in it. I had fun locating a lot of new servers that are not introduced in the main story although i'm not sure if i got all of them; sometimes, the secret is so well hidden that you have to read really carefully.

Pros:
- Uses mostly real terminal commands
- 2 branching paths
- Lots of secrets to explore

Cons:
- Leaving the server during a trace is kinda buggy
- You need to read a lot

[h1]Conclusions[/h1]
This is a nice hacking simulation game to spend your time with.

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to play hacking simulation game, buy this. You might have to know a little bit about terminals though; you can actually play it without knowing it at all but it might give you a harder time, especially if you don't like to learn and read.[/i]

The game will usually tell you whether you have to connect to a proxy, guess a firewall, run one of your hacking tools to open a number of port required to get in, or all of them. Sometimes, the server owner will notice your break in and a timer will show up. You must finish your hacking, remove your traces, and logout before it reaches zero or you'll get a blue screen. The strange thing is, the game is a bit "buggy" on this. If you leave the server while running your hacking tools, the hacking will still be ongoing and you can do your second attempt with a head start. The stranger thing is, if the timer reach zero by the time you finish the hacking (and you haven't logged out yet), the hacking will also be finished after you deal with the blue screen and return to the server. Well, there are actually some more, but these two are the only thing that i had in my mind for now. Since you'll use a lot of hacking tools, you might run out of memories. Some hacking tools take more memories than the others so you can't use them all at the same time. This helps to make the game more difficult although there is one place where you have to "cheat" your way through because you will never have the time to get in in the first place [spoiler](the CCC Hacksquad Filedump)[/spoiler]. The game's story has a two branching paths that will converge in the end. The other path requires you to really know what you're doing though; i won't be able to make it in if i didn't read a guide beforehand. The game also has some commands that are not available in help commands that might be useful in these cases. These additional commands are told after you beat the game and is supposed to be an additional command in case there is a new update in. You'll mostly play the game by accepting quests and finishing them. There is also a few points in the game where you can choose the missions that you want to do. Sadly, there is a place where you can't choose them all and it kinda saddens me since it left the place with unfinished tasks. Since you'll be hacking a lot of servers, there are some optional places that you can go to and some places might have some secrets in it. I had fun locating a lot of new servers that are not introduced in the main story although i'm not sure if i got all of them; sometimes, the secret is so well hidden that you have to read really carefully. Pros: - Uses mostly real terminal commands - 2 branching paths - Lots of secrets to explore Cons: - Leaving the server during a trace is kinda buggy - You need to read a lot [h1]Conclusions[/h1] This is a nice hacking simulation game to spend your time with. [h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1] [b]Yes.[/b] [i]If you like to play hacking simulation game, buy this. You might have to know a little bit about terminals though; you can actually play it without knowing it at all but it might give you a harder time, especially if you don't like to learn and read.[/i]

An absolutely engaging and wonderful game. This is one of those gems that lingers in your library for a while ominously taunting you. I'm going to break this review up in a few sections. With that in mind this game plays more like an information-gathering puzzle simulator.

1. Gameplay
This may be the biggest "fear" new players may have after viewing the trailer. This game involves typing out commands in a terminal, but really it's just similar to a "text based" adventure with commands. If you're new to using a CMD line (terminal) this is a perfect engaging way to become more familiar with how it works. Just like any new game once you get familiar with the controls you'll breeze through it. There is a clean graphic user interface that makes navigating the game environment (with your mouse) very intuitive. You are taught how to play in a standard tutorial so you're not just thrown out into the ocean expecting to be a 1337 h@ck0r. You will encounter several high and low points that will continue to test what you've learned. At no point in the game did I feel like it was repetitive. You will have time to become familiar with your tools and soon after your tools will grow, allowing you to tackle harder and more complex hacker challenges. 

2. Story
No spoilers. I can say that there is a story and that you will be highly involved with in. There is a lot of mysteries, and plenty of interesting characters to learn about. I should mention that each new play through of the game will have many events randomized. In addition the story continues in the DLC and that I found it totally worth it.

3. Graphics
I find the graphics to be a nice blend between modern techno sci-fi and retro website design. It's actually quite an interesting blend of styles that seems to work out well. I can safely say this [b]isn't[/b] just a game where you look into singular black box and type commands. 

4. Final Thoughts
It's good. I personally had some doubts but once I started playing I couldn't stop. I wouldn't be leaving a review if I didn't think it deserved more attention.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Hacknet [/h1]
[b] An interface so real, you probably shouldn't play it in public [/b]

[h1] Run-through [/h1]

Hacknet is a storytelling, hacking simulation game developed by Team Fractal Alligator and Published by Fellow Traveller. Featuring programming puzzles, intense challenges, and an amazing soundtrack, it's time to dive into the deepest corners of the web.

With the death of the hacker "Bit", you're suddenly dragged in the underground world of the hacking community. Contacted by his failsafe system, Bit sends you very specific instructions so that Hacknet-OS, the security system he created, won't fall in the wrong hands. Acting as the spiritual successor to Uplink, Hacknet adds story and spice to mere actions and command lines.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

• Amazing story
• Simplistic and easy to navigate UI. You can do everything the game asks you to without ever having to switch tabs up
• Challenging and entertaining puzzles
• The music feels always on point with the situation
• Mod support
• Tons of fun little Easter Eggs

[h1] Cons: [/h1]

• The tutorial is by all means too short and the game's content too wide. Might feel daunting for some players approaching the genre
• As most hacking games, don't expect accurate hacking sequences

[h1] Gameplay: in depth [/h1]

[u][b] General information [/b][/u]
Hacknet is one of those games that tend to surprise you in the best way possible. It's a game that I approached really carefully and ended up playing for hours on. The mystery around Bit's death is the most important part of the story, indeed, but Hacknet does an amazing job in giving us a handful of side missions and side stories to enrich our experience with. In our pursuit of the truth, in fact, we will stumble upon many different factions of Hackers, each of them acting accordingly to their own creeds - for example, there's a faction that wishes for people to perceive hackers as "decent" people rather than being demonised, a faction that just acts on whims and another that takes only the best hackers under its protective wing and offers them a proper job.

Even though Hacknet presents itself as a hacking game, it's quite obvious that we can't expect it to be 100% accurate on how it tackles the thematic: hacking servers and personal computers is actually really easy and requires the use of just about four or five command lines. It's clear that Hacknet's puzzle aspect comes from being able to understand what the missions are asking us to do at every given time, other than being able to enter said servers. Hacknet is a game that requires the player to be attentive and read carefully through every folder once we've hacked a device. Useful information hides everywhere.

There's a huge spectrum of missions to pick from: tinkering with websites strings, entering someone's personal mobile device, adding a degree to a student from their university's site, putting someone's names in the deceased list records and so on so forth.

Even though the game feels very linear, it is far from that. There are a lot of hidden riddles that will present you with extra hacking challenges and reward you with useful .exe files upon completing them. Successfully entering the CSEC also awards you with the ThemeChanger.exe, whereas you felt like customizing your x-system.exe program.

The soundtrack is perhaps the most enjoyable part of the whole game, by far. It's amazing how it always fits perfectly. It's relaxing if you're just skimming through the available servers, it picks up if you're hacking and you're about to get traced, it's got funny tunes if you stumble upon mini-games.

Overall, a nice experience with engaging content and features. Will rarely ever feeling boring as you're driven on by the need to know what truly happened and, of course, to become the best hacker out there.

[u][b] Content [/b][/u]
Hacknet offers a good spectrum of activities throughout the game. However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay.

[h1] Technical Analysis [/h1]

[u][b] Graphics [/b][/u]
A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else.
Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text.

[u][b] Music [/b][/u]
For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions.

[u][b] HUD [/b][/u]
The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable.
To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other.

[u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u]
None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done.

[h1] Wrapping up [/h1]

Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for.


[h1] RATING: 8.5/10 [/h1]

review_text_raw:
[i]Note: I am biased because of the nature of my job. While not related to IT Security, it involves technical troubleshooting / problem solving and all kind of investigations. Basically, less fun version of Hacknet.[/i]

[h3]Accurate Hacking Simulator?[/h3]

I was not exposed to a lot of hacking in games, maybe just a bit in Sleeping Dogs, or Cyberpunk 2077. While other games focus purely on hacking vibes, those tend to ignore the actual process. And Hacknet pays much more attention to the realistic aspect of the game.

Of course, to me it looks like huge oversimplification, but that was made as a game, right? It was made to be simple, fun and accessible. And it never felt like I am working, it felt like I am playing a game and having a good time. So while not being accurate, it nails the realistic hacking experience to enough extent. 

[h3]Handholding or Exploration?[/h3]

The first 60% to 70% percent of the game felt like a tutorial. Fun, with a lot of stories and action, but with a huge sense that I am playing in a sandbox. Everything is pretty safe, and you get what you need to do right from the email, so you need to execute specific steps without much investigation. Yes, you need to look for something specific, but it is usually very algorithmic and follows the same steps. 

So, this feels like handholding to me, and having to "detective" part to it, where you just don't know where to look at and have to think and explore. 

But! There are endgame quests, such as the main story line or Project Junebug quest. Those actually did things perfectly as I have wanted. There is more to reading, investigating, searching and connecting pieces of information together. This was perfect. 

Example: usually it would be "find a (file / password / IP) or edit / remove something. Here is the server.". That is straightforward. 

Project Junebug: Here is the name of the person. Kill him.

review_text_raw:
In [i]Hacknet[/i], you play as a computer user who has just been bestowed a unique operating system (OS) with tools that can hack different computers. As the game progresses, you will discover new hacking tools, join other factions of hackers, fulfill hacking job contracts to build your reputation, and solve the game’s central mystery.

What I love about [i]Hacknet[/i] is the high level of immersion and engaging pacing. With my headphones on, listening to the adrenaline-pumping soundtrack, I voraciously took on one hacking contract after another. Before long, two to three hours have flown by. The game's missions, though all require hacking, vary in objects and pacing. Because of that, I did not find gameplay repetitive, and I used every opportunity to familiarize myself with the tools I had at my disposal. All of this prepared me for the climatic final mission, which totally did not disappoint.

[i]Hacknet[/i] is novice-friendly, but some players may find it having a slightly steep learning curve. Players will be at an advantage if they can type fast, has used *nix (e.g. Linux) shell commands, and/or are familiar with text-based OSes. This is because the user interface of [i]Hacknet[/i] is austere, with typing as your primary form of input. Still, there are simple graphics to depict hacking progress, network of computers, and directory trees. You can use your mouse from time to time as means of in-game navigation as I did.

[i]Hacknet[/i]'s appeal aside from immersion and pacing is really its simplicity. The players will always be given all the tools they would need to complete missions. So, the real challenge is to figure out which tool(s) to use to hack the computers and phones, and to do it quickly and efficiently. So, think fast! Type fast and furious! Once the dust has settled, snooping around the hacked machines and reaping your rewards are gratifying.

At the time of this review, [i]Hacknet[/i] is my favourite hacking-themed game. It’s fast, it’s empowering, and it’s extremely gratifying -- especially after a challenging mission. I highly recommend this game to those who wish an adrenaline-pumping, brain-teasing, text-based adventure game.

review_text_raw:
***This only takes the base game into account***

Ever wanted to crack down on some real terminal action to get a peek at what this hacking business is all about? Wonder no more, as Hacknet is here to "teach" you what "hacking" is. 

Immersive, intelligent and just enough unix-commands at your disposal, Hacknet will convince anyone not computer savvy or not paying close enough attention that the things on your monitor sure looks like something you shouldn't be doing, almost like dark wizardry magic. For the most part, the game offers up this illusion at an convincing rate while being beginner-friendly. However, in the world of hacking, there is very little hand holding, so the faster you understand what the ropes are, the better.

To deliver a convincing hacking experience, music is paramount - as Uplink back in the day taught everyone. Here is really delivers, with everything from ambient barrens tunes fit for the breaks between each mission, to serious business from The Algorithm and wildly intense adrenaline pumping Carpenter Brut songs. Hats off, this album is even worth listening to way after you've finished the game. 

As for the the main story, while not top shelf, is interesting enough to keep searching around for clues and getting a better grasp at what's going. As with any self respecting game that depicts hacking, it should have its sheer selectino of surprise elements, and Hacknet doesn't disappoint. However, this is usually found in side missions. The main story should've done more of that as well.

For each time you play, the game changes up names, IPs etc for the nodes to try to keep things sort of fresh, but the missions are mostly the same. All in all, Hacknet is a very solid, albeit simple at times, attempt at creating an immersive, "real enough" hacking simulator that most importantly is -FUN-. The list of unix commands are however at times frustratingly limited, especially if you know what you're doing. Since most of the game is very well laid out in terms of the interface, you start taking it for granted that you should be able to do more than you actually are allowed to. 

For example, "rm file*" will not work since the terminal doesn't support wildcards. Pathing is also needlessly tedious, as it doesn't properly understand using root-nodes in paths. Props however for making it possible to furk up yourself, which is how it should be. Paying attention and going "outside the beaten path" is usually rewarded.
 
Hacknet requires reading and understanding of its core concepts to get the most out of the experience. For those persistent enough, the game also delivers some hilarious content as a nod to the efforts. Here's to hoping the developer makes more content to this game, as the main game is rather short. It'll take you only around 5-6 hours for the main campaign. A multiplayer mode would've been awesome in addition to random missions. 

Rating: 8/10 - Play it!

[h3][i]Ahem...[/i] [/h3]

I think it's time to finally write something about this game, with which I actually share quite a fun personal story. I received it as a gift from my close friend when I "finished" studying as a software engineer at a local college where I lived for some time. And when I actually began to play it, it ended just like my study. Disastrous! I was completely lost and confused, dropping the game after a while.

But the time passed, and my hands finally reached it again in 2024 when I began to clear up my gaming backlog. Finishing all that I missed or didn't play yet. Including this particular game. And what can I say? I actually finished it! I'm sure my teachers would be so proud of me! If I did it myself, that is... Which I didn't, obviously! Some things just never change... Certainly not my stupidity! But enough of self-embarrassing stories. Now about the game...

It really is that good! I never imagined that it'd have such a wild plot with an actual plot junction at some point. Not to mention it was actually fun to pester in other people's business via hacking and reading all their sensitive data. Found a few wild stories that way! In addition to learning something in the process! I already forgot what it was, but I certainly felt a bit brainy after I finished this game. At least for a bit...

So if you're really interested in something different and aren't afraid to bash your head during the process, give this game a try. It's quite unique in its own way! And don't be intimidated by it. There's quite a good guide to help you out if you're underwhelmed by it.

First of all, I never played Uplink, so I can't compare this to that. What I did play was the HackRUN saga, so please pardon my comparison to a not very similar game. I also think it's funny that there are .dll and .exe file on what is (seemingly) a Linux system, but I can ignore that.

In a nutshell, Hacknet is a hacking sim game with a decent storyline. That is something I don't see often. HackRUN also has a storyline, but it's pretty linear if you ask me. This game uses real UNIX commands. For those of you new to the coding world (I guess?), it won't be hard to pick up; the tutorial does a good job of introducing the commands, and the 'help' menu will always be there to help you. For those of you who are familiar with the UNIX command prompt, you will be pleasantly surprised. The animations you get when hacking is pretty cool too. The best part of this games\ is that there are some systems that will start tracing you once you start your hacks. You have 100 seconds to do whatever you need to do and GTFO the system, or else (I don't actually know what happens because I have never failed doing so). You can, disconnect midway to cut the trace short and come back in the system again to do your stuff (again) at a later time, but hey, where's the fun in that? Along the way of making yourself a name in the hacking world (in the game), you will encounter files that are seemingly unimportant (like IRC log files, random text files, etc.). You are half right, [b]most[/b] of these files are unimportant. They may contain jokes and the stupidity of internet friends chatting together; but the rest may contain passwords that will make your life much easier when attempting to access some systems or useful information on your target's location.

There are decent puzzles in this game that happens in a specific scenario, but the contracts you get are pretty repetitive: [spoiler]probe the system, bypass proxy/firewall if those are there, open some ports, hack in, do your stuff, clear logs, get out[/spoiler]. New commands are introduced every now and then, but those have instructions along with them, so it's pretty easy to do whatever you need to do after. Basically, it's not very challenging (unless the devs add a "No x-server" mode to force you to use the command prompt throughout the game, that would be really fun, devs pls read). The last thing that this game lacks is the ability to adjust the SFX volume. Me clicking things actually shocks me sometimes because trust me, the SFXs are loud.

In conclusion, Hacknet is a good hacking sim with a decent storyline and a bit of realism. Would I recommend? Yes. Would I play again? Yes.

If you reach this point, thank you for raking your time to read the massive wall of text that my review is (lol).

*Got the game for $2.99 during a sale*

Hacknet is an interesting game. Let's just get that out of the way. Its got a very good storyline and, while I have some experience in [strike]hacking[/strike] computer security, I didn't find (most) of the puzzles too difficult for the average person to solve. It sets a very good pace, picking up the difficulty very well. I'm writing this review just after completing the game, which took me just over 6 hours.

You start off with a message from Bit, telling you how to use the Hacknet software, etc. etc. Basically a tutorial on how to use it, the command line, that sort of thing. (If you're a linux user, this game will be much easier, the commands are basically the same for navigating the terminal and the like) After this, you're sent off to a hacker group, Entropy. You do a few hacks, and things start to pick up. You rise to the top (naturally) and start going off, investigating. I'd say more but I don't want to risk spoilers. The ending was very intriguing, and worth the effort.

The challenges are similar, but I never got bored of them. Find server at X IP, break down any proxies, firewalls, and open ports to use the almighty PortHack and get the admin password. Then, do whatever you need to, be it uploading or downloading a file, deleting stuff, or (later) even messing with databases and some... other devices. ([spoiler]a pacemaker[/spoiler]) They become more difficult as you progress, adding tracers that initiate an IP change failsafe if you take too long, more ports to open, and more complex firewalls and proxies. You'll need to grab passwords from emails and circumvent servers with powerful tracers, and even more interesting events. The only randomly difficult challenge that jumped me was an attack on my PC, which I was able to avoid using a [spoiler]trap shell[/spoiler]. If it gets you, there is a guide to help you out.

The interface is very intuitive and I never had any unreasonable issues with it, aside from becoming stuck when entering a password I didn't want to enter. (Which is my fault, I clicked login. What did I expect?) Later, you get the option to switch your layout, but none of them are really terrible. You have the terminal window (for commands), the display window (for showing the filesystem, passwords, databases, emails, etc.), the RAM window (watch this one, especially later when you get more RAM-hungry programs), and your NetMap (showing all the IPs you've connected to/can connect to).

The playtime was a good length. I would have liked it to be a bit longer but 6 hours is longer than AAA campaigns. God I hate AAA companies. Be innovative. Or I'll use Hacknet to take down your servers. /rant. Anyway, I'm not complaining about the length. As I said earlier, it never got repetitive, it was always interesting. There was always a sense of "oh gotta do this quickly or they're gonna catch me with that trace" that pushes you forward. Because of that speed though, don't play this game if you're not a quick typist. I have a speed of about 70 WPM (Faster now), which is well above average. I'd recommend being able to go above 40 WPM to play this effectively. 

------------------------------------------------------

review_text_raw:
As a lifelong computer geek nerd I have always sucked at coding and command line stuff. Back in school I was bad at languages and good at science, maths and creative stuff so I blame my sucky coding skills on this. 

I have however always been a fan of hacking games such as the Uplink and Hacker Evolution series but they have always felt more like hacking from the movie hackers rather than what actual hacking might be like. Hacknet is much closer to what I imagine it is like and I really enjoyed the time I spent with it. The game was easy to get into and moves at a decent pace with an intuitive difficulty curve that meant I never felt I knew exactly what to do but equally never floundered and got stuck.  

As far as I understand this isn’t really an accurate sim of any kind of software it is instead an adventure game with a DOS style command line interface. There are some graphical elements to help things along but the game, at least to an outsider, feels very real.

There were a few times that I got stuck but this was nothing that a few moments checking the help page did not fix. If anything one of the things I feel could have really benefitted this game would be multi-monitor support. It was really annoying to have to flick between windows as opposed to having multiple windows open at the same time. 

The game is relatively difficult but not unfair but I think someone with a better knowledge of command line interfaces might have found it easier.

As you progress through the game you begin to understand more about the world you live in as the story evolves in front of you. There are a fair amount of pop culture references that always raise a smile. 

Overall Hack Net is well worth playing to anyone who watched hackers or Jurassic Park and wanted to feel like they were shit hot at computering.

review_text_raw:
A hacker named Bit is dead. His computer had an automated script which sends a random person a set of instructions. YOU are the one selected to follow out his last will.

The game is a good hacking simulation, with a good command line system, a well-designed UI for those who aren't quite used to the command line yet, and a very well-designed web of connections. IP addresses, names, and quests are randomized each time so everyone's experience is slightly different. They even have some funny conversations in text files on some PCs. All the scripts you need to complete the game are easily accessible, whether you get them from hidden locations or you find them in organization databases. There are even some interesting things you can do with the command line and some interesting moments where it pays to have a bit of extra knowledge going in. And easter eggs. MANY easter eggs. Seriously, when you think you've found it all, something new catches your eye.

Through my playthroughs I did not check if there was a way to create automated scripts for some of these things. If it was possible, I completely missed it, and if it wasn't, it is something I would fault this game for at least slightly. However, it not being there does not detract from the rest of the game, as hacking tools are abundant. The story is really good, and all of the design moments know just how to kick your brain into overdrive.

Overall, I'd give it a 10/10. This is one of my favorite games to date. If you are willing to learn the command line, generally good practices, and pay close attention to everything you find, this game will be a blast. I HIGHLY recommend learning how to use the command line instead of relying on the UI, as there are some things that will definitely be much better if you do so. A second or third playthrough also still hits pretty good, as you can look back at when things were introduced, catch things you wouldn't have caught before, and overall experience it in a completely different way. After you've played the DLC and the game itself once or twice though, the replayability goes down heavily, but there is a TON of mods in the community if you want to see what others have made.

Go out there and leave no trace behind.

review_text_raw:
A very introspective look at UNIX commands and the general actions of hacking - which is basically accurate, but taking out the time required to accomplish these things (for example, you can solve port protocols within a few seconds, but IRL this might take hours).

Basically, if you want the "reality" where you are the hacker in one of these movies (you're not playing the hacker, but ARE the hacker), then this is pretty spot-on. It just removes most of the tedium of the acitivites. This is not to say that the game isn't repetitive; it is, and remains true to its roots as a simulator. By nature, most simulators run off of repetitive actions which require muscle memory and timing in order to complete.

In actual fact, this is more of a puzzle-solving game. However, combined with some funny easter eggs (IRC chats can get hilarious) and honest-to-god methodology on the principles of hacking, this actually becomes enjoyable unless you just want to shoot things in the face (in which case, this is NOT the game for you).

Anyone who wants to work in software QA should be able to play this game comfortably, figure out most of the puzzles, and genuinely enjoy the experience. If you can't, don't take QA as a career. Because this in almost any form is what you do - all day, every day. I know this from 14 years of experience at that job in everything from game development to SAS or security software.

There are a few points I wish there were more of, or more developed. As game, it's pretty linear. There are nice little things like finding additional information on a server which gives you another terminal to hack, or a phone to break into, but these are too few and far between. It could be far more sandboxy if there were a freeform mode for points, which had sets of systems and connected devices which would allow you to randonly investigate things you found on another system. In this, you'd need a points system or something to gain (money, cred, whatever) - which would be a welcome addition to the game. I think another fun mode would be to actually use the system specs for the computer it was running on for memory, etc. as well as randonly generating in-game groups to become involved with, do missions for (from forums, etc.)

I recommend this game, just due to the simulation nature being captured very well. That being said, this game won't be for everyone. Much of the game is tedium and random investigation - which is exactly what hacking is about. One of the best missions which represents this is the "Project Junebug" mission. You're basically let loose to figure out how to accomlish the task, you have a lot of reading to do to catch up on how to accomplish it, and there isn't any handholding. YOU have to do the tasks, to the best of your understanding, and figure out indeed, what those tasks are, and it involves multiple servers, and different methods of having the same outcome.

review_text_raw:
Pros:

1. It's simple and pretty straight forward
2. You never (mostly) are left in the dark about what to do next
3. You can be a "real" Hacker for once
4. Simple and understandable UI
5. Learn some Linux commands
6. Great Storyline
7. The atmosphere and tense you get while hacking
8. A lot of hidden ingame stuff
9. The DLC "Labyrinths"

Neutral:

1. I can imagine that the music is not for everyone
2. Way too simple and straight forward compared to Uplink
3. Limited Options (while in Uplink you can hack Banks to get money or even give it to someone else, destory/save lives by manipulating police entries and such)
4. Missing does insane minigames, from Uplink, to crack a Lan and the option to build your own computersetup 

In-Depth Review:

I don't know if people still know that gem of a game called "Uplink". It's from the Year 2001 and was one of the best science fiction games back then (still is, but didnt aged very well). Hacknet is just a modern version of "Uplink". But it's extremly simplified compared to it, which have it's pros and it's cons of being so ofc. While Hacknet never reaches that incredible Depth Uplink offered, it's still have a lot of great moments itself, mostly because of a good storyline you can follow.

Hacknet is basically a pure text-based game in a science fiction setting. You are hacking computers, databases and other stuff 100% of the time. You wont do anything else. Don't except to buy your own computerparts, or anything like that. Playtime is around 10-20 hours and more if you have the DLC. 

The game is pretty easy and very straight forward. I have the feeling the game is holding your hands for a bit too long. But when it finally let you loose, oh boy, the felling of power and control is just awesome. There so many secrets to discover and little hidden stuff to look out for, it keeps you occupied for a few hours. And the music (it varies, but sometimes it's psytrance-like music and you get the felling you are on a Goa-Party) is pushing you all the time. You really fell like a "Supa Hacka" at times.

If you like the basegame, check out the DLC "Labyrinths" as well, because it lets you loose right from the start. It offers a own storyline to follow, new features, executables and Themes. 

Overall Hacknet and it's DLC, surely is worth the money if you like text-based adventures, want to learn/relearn a few basic Linux/Dos commands on the way, looking for a new Uplink for years (like myself), or just want to be a "Supa Hacka" for once.

The hacking mechanics are gamified, but still based on real programs, attacks, and port numbers.  I've used a lot of command line, and muscle memory actually helped me in the game!

[i]Hacknet[/i] is described as “an immersive, terminal-based hacking simulator” wherein the person playing HacknetSSthe game – you, yourself, sitting at your computer – is the closest thing to a protagonist. It presents you with a Linux-like OS, an electronica soundtrack, and a command prompt. In reality, it isn’t far removed from Kali Linux, a distribution of the open source operating system favored by security professionals and hackers alike.

Most of the game takes place inside that command prompt, where a minimalistic tutorial teaches the player how to list files in a directory, copy and remove files, and run executables. Once the basics are established, the game goes on to provide the player with tidbits of knowledge, such as how to remove traces of your presence on a compromised system, as well as in-game analogues to real-world programs that execute buffer overflow attacks, password cracks, and network mapping.

I would go so far as to recommend [i]Hacknet[/i] to anyone interested in network and information security work as a way of gauging their real interest in the field; [i]Hacknet[/i] is simply that good.

[h1]8/10[/h1]

Hacknet is a pretty entertaining hacking game for those that have an interest to stay long enough or of the genre.

To start, hacknet has a nice flow of events. The story is rather compelling and starts off fast. You are literally thrown into the events right away. The hacking is also somewhat similar to how the events would go in real life (to a degree of course) as some of this stuff is also what real life hackers employ from what I know. There are also interesting and funny parts of this game. At a certain point I remember hacking into a certain system and reading the logs. One of the logs was the top searched terms, and they were all like "Boobs" "Big Boobs" and stuff like that. The music for this game is also pretty good and fitting.

There are bad parts of this game as well. The biggest bad part is when you get hacked and are thrown into a screen without any directions to do anything. I was so confused at that point that I had to look at a guide to know what the hell was going on. Another bad part of this game is that its hard to get back into if you stop playing, as in it's hard to pick back up since some of the things are rather specific and easy to forget if you drop it for some time. The game really doesn't have a particularly good transition from tutorial to game mode as well. Although you get to practice it a lot because there are a ton of hacking missions.

Overall, pretty good hacking game, but it is more meant for those interested in this genre.

Rating: 7.8/10
Recommend Price: $2.49 or lower.

I recommended this game to my little brother, who is currently studying programming in university. It went like this:

Me: Hey, you should check out this game called Hacknet. It's about hacking into other people's PCs and doing various tasks, it has a story, and I think you'll find it funny.
Bro: Huh, does it, like, imitate actual hacking?
Me: ...you run PortHack.exe to connect to other systems.
Bro: *gives a sarcastic thumbs up*

Hacknet is fun and has a nice soundtrack. The story is OK and the puzzles aren't very challenging except for that one... but maybe I'm just not very smart. The game is also quite short, I was done with it in like 6 or so hours.

Hacking works like so: you have a set of "keys" - programs you run to break the "locks" on a system before you can PortHack into it to get control over that node. You start without any "key" and get them as you progress through the story.
The story is given to you through emails you receive in-game, and you advance it by doing tasks from specific people or special quest boards.
The difficulty is... You always have all the info and tools you need to deal with your current puzzles. Remember this. Sometimes people even remind you how some (easier) things are done. Then there's that one (avoidable, you may not trigger it) thing where you have to do something completely new which you got no instructions for. Or maybe I'm just dumb.
The game also quotes bash.org a lot.

Obviously, this game isn't for everyone. review_text_raw:
So first and foremost: As someone who works with computer systems as a profession, I must admit that I am one of the few odd ones that really, *really* dislikes terminal based stuff. That being said, this game not only forced me to use the terminal, but actually gave me a reason to get used to using it, which has helped with my work. 

This game is enjoyable, extremely so. Going into this game with mixed feelings, especially with what I felt, at the time, was the most important plot element being spoiled (Bit's death) I wasn't really sure how to feel about it, but I quickly forgot all about that as I began tackling missions and getting used to the world. On my first day alone I clocked nearly 6 hours of game time, which is almost half of the time that I've spent on this game to date so far. I simply could not put it down. While it's not completely realistic, the concept is really well executed and it's definitely one of the more real hacking themed games that I've seen compared to others.

The game play starts off rather simple, and there isn't really much challenge in the beginning, but for those who aren't really computer savvy this gives them time to learn how to do some of the essentials while also testing their skills and improving. I think the first time I actually struggled was after getting counter-hacked by Naix and getting thrown into Terminal Mode, although I was freaking out over that because up until that point I had been really successful at avoiding any security in place; I was confused as I was positive that I had deleted everything in the logs dir and couldn't understand how I had been found. I wasn't aware that it was a scripted sequence until later. 

One thing I wish the game did a bit better though was when you failed to DC in time and were tracked. There was *so* much going on in the short amount of time you have to reset your IP that the first time it happened to me, I panicked and almost failed, resorting to closing out of the game (because what is cheating, right?). 

While there are a few issues with the game's missions, namely you being unable to complete missions if you've managed to wonder off to another one, overall I feel the game is extremely polished for something that started off as a small project. The missions are all enjoyable, the music is fantastic, the story is overall impressive (and the small logs scattered throughout the computers is a pretty enjoyable addition as well), and it just feels good as a whole. I haven't gotten around to playing the DLC yet, but if it's anything like the rest of the main game, I'm sure it won't disappoint in the slightest.

I would strongly recommend this to anyone who is looking for a bit of a more "realistic" hacking game. It makes you think, and teaches you some terminal basics, all while having fun in the process.
